hypothesis: Step 6 first run: bundle 26 finds the boot clock words after the ROM return that follows bundle 25
conclusion: The boot ROM resets CPU-L and the DSU but not CPU-B. Fix adopted: never return with CPU-B raised; every image that raises CPU-B lowers it to 1014 MHz before a successful return (see the design). The rails kept their voltages across the return.
narrative:
Run record: board-session-cpu-top-opp-7/port-3-3, set step6-set-2. Bundle 25 left CPU-B at 2002 MHz, CPU-L at 1794 MHz and the DSU at 1274 MHz, with DCDC3 at 1050 mV and DCDC5 at 1000 mV. The rails kept their voltages.
Explanation: the boot ROM's clock setup programs two PLLs from its literal pool: 0x08871000 (CPU-L) and 0x08873000 (DSU), through the routine at 0x1898 that calls the PLL writer at 0x1774 once for each with N = 38, then selects both muxes at 0x1af0. The pool holds no 0x08872000 and no routine writes CPU-B (a8e31821, literals at 0x1f78 to 0x1fa0; docs/vendor-firmware/boot-rom-and-boot0.md). CPU-B's boot word 0xf8802700 (N = 39, 1014 MHz) comes from boot0's board setup, which the cold DDR start runs once per lifetime. Every earlier lifetime had lowered CPU-B to 1014 MHz before its return (steps 1 and 4).
Alternatives weighed: accept a raised CPU-B after a return (bundle 26 and the relock accept the top word with the rail at 1050 mV), which would persist through every later image and require each to know it (an image that lowers DCDC3, B1's baseline defined at boot0's rate, and the step images admitting only CPU-B at 1014 MHz); or never return with CPU-B raised (chosen). Under the chosen rule bundle 25 does not change CPU-B (it raises DCDC5 through CPU-L's top point and DCDC3 with CPU-B held at 1014 MHz, the change step 3 qualified); the workload's relock raises CPU-B and, on the completed path after all seven secondaries are OFF, CPU0 lowers CPU-B to 1014 MHz (N = 39) at EL3 with the relock's own sequence before the return (top_opp_lower_b in boot/a733/top-opp-relock.c); bundle 27 then only reads the boot words.

conclusion: The prediction was wrong because of the baseline, not the clocks or the measurement. The boot-rate runs used native image 762237cd, not 6fd7af86 that step 6 runs. The two images' background loops are identical (an exclusive increment of the core's counter between two calls of ucPortGetCoreID) but that routine differs: in 762237cd it is a supervisor call from the EL0 task, in 6fd7af86 it reads TPIDRRO_EL0 and returns. At the boot rates the old image spends about 188 cycles per iteration on the A55 cores and 248 on the A76 cores, the new one about 23 and 20 (32 ms window of 32 ticks). Against the correct baseline the counts scale 3.85 times on the A55 cores (clock ratio 1794/494 = 3.63) and 2.06 times on the A76 cores (2002/1014 = 1.97), about 6% and 4% above the clock ratios; a fixed amount of other work per window (rounds, tick, SGIs) explains it: fitting count = k (f W - O) to both rates with W = 32 ms gives O = 1.21 million cycles (2.4 ms at 494 MHz) on the A55 cores and 2.62 million cycles (2.6 ms at 1014 MHz) on the A76 cores, and 21 and 19 cycles per iteration. Both core types lose about the same 2.5 ms at the boot rates. The A76/A55 count ratio is 2.30 at the boot rates (clock ratio 2.05) and 1.23 at the top points (clock ratio 1.12): an A76 core runs 1.10 to 1.12 times as many iterations per cycle as an A55 core; the predicted 0.85 came from the wrong baseline.

The helper lowers DCDC3 with CPU-B held, then DCDC5 with CPU-L and the DSU held; either rail may enter at any voltage from 800 mV to the bin's top point on that rail, so the helper also restores the rails a failed top-point image leaves while the three CPU domains read their boot PLL and mux words; a rail already at 800 mV gets no write (checks/cpu-rails-return.c, checks/os-cpu-return-rails.py). For an image that links the CPU-return entry guard, tools/dev-run.py runs it by default before the launch and after a normal return. After any other outcome DRAM can be uninitialized and the helper launch uses DRAM over FEL, so cold DDR comes first and the next launch lowers the rails.
